title: The years and the days
hook: the years teach much which the days never know (Experience)

segments.voice: Yesterday, grief that teaches nothing: Emerson refusing to turn his son's death into a lesson. Your line was it taught nothing. Was there room today to let something stay unexplained? Day one thousand two hundred six.

An old photo turns up, taken about this time last year. A kitchen, a face, a sky. Where was that, again? What was going on that week? The particular day is mostly gone. But the year it belonged to has a shape now that it didn't have back then: what started, what ended, what turned out to matter and what didn't. Emerson put that difference into a single sentence, in the same essay as yesterday's grief. Today, one plain sentence about time.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM LAST YEAR.` → `THE DAY IS GONE.` → `THE YEAR HAS A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Experience, Emerson writes: "The years teach much which the days never know." Read it slowly. The years teach. The days never know. Second, why the days can't know. A single day is too close to see. Inside it you're answering messages, making dinner, worrying about a meeting. You can see the weather, not the climate. A choice that will change everything can look, on the day, like a small errand: a phone call returned, a class signed up for, a door knocked on. Nothing in that day announces what it is. Third, why the years can. Distance does what closeness can't. Seen from a year or more away, the scattered days take on a shape. Patterns show. The worry that filled a whole month shrinks to a footnote, and a quiet habit you barely noticed turns out to have carried you. That kind of knowledge isn't available on the day. It has to be waited for. Fourth, how it sits next to yesterday. Yesterday Emerson said his grief taught him nothing. Today, from the same essay, the years teach much. He doesn't tie the two together, and it would be wrong to say he does. But a reader can hold both: a day of loss may teach nothing at all, and it doesn't have to. Whatever the years teach, they teach slowly. The practical gift in that is patience. Today doesn't have to make sense today.
screen: `THE YEARS TEACH MUCH.` · `A DAY IS TOO CLOSE TO SEE.` · `DISTANCE GIVES THE DAYS A SHAPE.` · `THE SAME ESSAY AS YESTERDAY.` · then, large: `THE DAYS NEVER KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back over one year. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind go back to about this time last year. Where were you living? What were you worried about? Who was close? Then come forward slowly, season by season, without judging any of it. Notice one thing that looked small then and turned out to matter, or one worry that turned out to be smaller than it seemed. Just notice. The bell holds the time.
The years and the days. Emerson's line in Experience: the years teach much which the days never know. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the years teach. When something today doesn't make sense, give it room, and let the years have their turn to explain it. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: Readers often reach for this line from Emerson's Experience at birthdays, new years and anniversaries, as a reminder that some things can only be understood from a distance.
